school-mode.note: CORRECTED 2026-08-25 in two directions at once. First, the stale claim: this note used to say the school-status control "declares action:'school-status' which App does not answer yet, so the control is present and inert" -- App.tsx line 1956 does answer it (`if (action === 'school-status') return this.schoolStatusLine;`), and schoolStatusLine is set from schoolModeActive() on mount (line 1052), so the control genuinely reports live state; it was never inert by the time that sentence was written, only stale. Second, the real gap the old note buried under that stale claim: school-mode.ts exports the visibility filter this feature is named for -- capabilityVisible(), filterVisibleCapabilities(), effectiveLanguageMode(), effectiveFunnyLevel(), HIDDEN_CAPABILITIES -- and none of them are imported by App.tsx. What App.tsx does import and genuinely wire is the switch itself: activateSchoolMode, deactivateSchoolMode, hasCredential, renameSchoolMode, schoolModeActive, schoolModeName, setCredential, all called from real control handlers, all covered by the credential-consumption design described below. So turning School mode on and off is real, renaming it is real, the credential gate is real -- but the mode's whole point per its own contract ("forces plain English presentation and makes ... every optional or playful capability behave as though uninstalled") never happens: schoolModeActive() is read only to build the status line, never to gate a language choice, a funny level, or any capability's visibility. Activating School mode currently changes nothing except what the status control says. Honest about being a presentation lock rather than a security boundary, including that deleting the shared local record resets it. 32 tests. NOTE: this lane also added five controls to the design and recompiled the renderer, which was outside the file boundary it was given; the edit inserted cleanly ahead of the Fun group and destroyed nothing, and the drift guard passes, so it is kept. The credential surface is a bound field plus app/renderer/src/credential-field.ts, which CONSUMES it: the secret is taken and the field blanked in the same step, so its life in component state is one call long. That matters because a bound control value is walked by exports, by the settings surfaces and by anything that dumps or screenshots state -- a secret merely sitting there has already left through several doors. The earlier draft used window.prompt, which Electron does not implement and which would have thrown at runtime with no unit test catching it. Turning the mode on needs nothing and turning it off needs the credential, so the two directions deliberately do not share a path. A rejected attempt never reveals whether a credential is even set, no message quotes what was typed, and every message uses the chosen name rather than the shipped one.

external-settings-sources.note: Implemented 2026-08-24 as app/renderer/src/external-settings-sources.ts: URL validation, response validation and the settings a response is permitted to change, for both an HTTPS API and a Home Assistant boolean entity. Written defensively because a settings value arriving over the network is an input from a system nobody here controls. HTTPS only except an explicitly bounded loopback development route, since http anywhere else sends the accompanying token in the clear; no credentials in the URL, because a URL reaches logs and error messages; redirects refused, since a redirect is the far end choosing a destination this console never validated; responses size-capped and JSON-parsed defensively; only allowlisted keys read, and only string values, because coercing a number would be this console deciding what a remote system meant. An answer carrying an older generation is dropped, so a slow reply from the previous poll cannot land after a fast one and flip a setting back with nothing to explain it. A Home Assistant "off" is an ordinary state rather than a failure. An unreachable source keeps the last known good values and says the person’s own settings are untouched underneath, because the one thing a remote source must never do is become the base.Wired end to end 2026-08-24. A person configures a source on the Settings sources group; App polls each one on its own timer through the settings.source.fetch action; the privileged process makes the request because it needs the token; the renderer decides what the answer may change; and the applied values go through baseSetVal, the same path a manual edit takes. A stored source is treated as untrusted input on the way back IN as well as out -- the file is hand-editable, and a source whose allowlist went missing would sit in the list looking configured while permitting anything a response offered, so it is dropped rather than loaded. One bad entry drops itself and not the list. A corrupt file yields no sources rather than throwing on mount, because losing the list is recoverable and failing to start is not. A source that has stopped working is named in the status with the reason and the time, since silently ceasing to track is the failure this feature exists to avoid.

status-hub.note: Implemented 2026-08-24 as app/renderer/src/status-hub-client.ts: the report a console sends about its own state, and the rules for refusing to send a claim it cannot support. A lane claiming passed or failed with no evidence is refused, because those are the two states a reader acts on and a lane claiming either with nothing to check is what makes a status page worse than none. `unrun` is a state of its own rather than a synonym for failed, since a check nobody ran reported as failed sends somebody hunting a defect that does not exist. Every field is named explicitly when the payload is built rather than spread, because a session is assembled from state that also holds credentials, hostnames and vault keys. And a reply cursor older than the hub still holds resynchronises and REPORTS the gap, because retrying asks the same impossible question forever and skipping means somebody’s answer was never acted on. The Status hub screen's own ‘Record this session’ button (App.tsx onBuildHubSession, landed 2026-08-26) is now a real consumer: it builds a SessionReport from this window's own state -- one lane per config screen this run has tried to read, passed/failed with real evidence, never invented -- validates it with validateReport, and lists the buildPayload result as a row on the screen. What remains genuinely unbuilt is the network half: this console has no privileged HTTP client, no configured hub address and no session key, so a recorded session is never transmitted anywhere, and the button and the screen both say so plainly. Real remote consumption still needs the same shape the settings source now has -- a fetcher in the process that owns the credential vault, a dispatch action reaching it, and a surface to configure the hub -- plus a poll that reports on a timer and reads the reply inbox with the cursor advanceCursor() already resynchronises against.

app-logo-customization.note: Wired 2026-08-24 with four controls: shipped presets, a picture of your own, one-action reset, and a status line naming the mark actually in use. The file is read in the renderer from the File the picker hands over, which needs no new privilege -- an input already opens the platform dialog, and a main-process reader would have given the window the ability to open anything else. Only the head is read, because discovering a file is too large by reading all of it does the expensive thing before the cheap check; the size comes from the File rather than from that capped read, since a capped read reports the cap and every oversized file would then measure exactly the limit and pass. Dimensions come from the header before anything decodes, which is the only ordering under which the pixel bound catches a decompression bomb at all. A rejected picture leaves the previous mark exactly as it was and says so.

command-palette.note: Wired 2026-08-24. Ctrl+Shift+F from anywhere, captured rather than bubbled so a field that stops key propagation cannot swallow the one chord meant to work everywhere. The list is DERIVED from the compiled design -- every destination, every setting on every screen, every appearance control -- because a hand-written palette is a second inventory of the same thing and the two diverge the first time somebody adds a control, always with the palette as the stale one. Plain text matching, case-insensitive, never a pattern: regex is an explicit opt-in everywhere else, and a palette treating a typed dot as any-character would return the wrong thing rather than nothing. Starts-with beats contains beats detail-only, stably, so a familiar result stops moving between keystrokes. Selecting a setting opens its screen and then scrolls and focuses the exact row through a data-ctl hook added to the design control template -- landing on the right screen and leaving somebody to hunt is not teleporting, and when the row genuinely is not on display it says so rather than silently doing nothing. Closed, it is absent from the document entirely, so nothing of it is tabbable or readable by a screen reader; Escape returns focus to whatever had it.

accessibility.note: Implemented 2026-08-24 as app/renderer/src/accessibility-contract.ts: WCAG relative luminance and contrast ratio from hex with the AA and AAA thresholds, target-size checking including a visually small control with adequate padded hit area, accessible-name resolution refusing a name whose only source is a decorative glyph, focus-indicator and positive-tabindex checks, and a reduced-motion resolver where either the platform preference or the app setting asking for less motion wins. Every threshold is a named constant citing its source. 37 tests. Wired 2026-08-24 into the appearance editor, which is where a person picks a colour and therefore where a contrast measurement is worth having. The ap_contrast readout reports the real WCAG ratio for the accent being chosen against the console’s own surface, taken from the compiled design’s root background rather than guessed, and it reuses the same colour translator the panel itself shows so the measured value is the one on screen rather than a second conversion. It reports the ratio as well as the level, because "fail" alone does not say whether a colour is slightly short or hopeless, and it distinguishes passing for large text only. It reports and never refuses: a colour that fails AA is still the person’s to keep, but they should not have to discover it is unreadable by trying to read it.

responsive-sizing.note: styles.css carries real width breakpoints at 1200px and 1000px: the section list narrows, the icon rail narrows from 88px to 72px, and every compiled grid collapses to a single flexed column. They are forced overrides because the compiled interface writes literal pixel values into inline style strings, which no external selector can otherwise beat. Building them found a real clipping defect at the app's own 920px floor, where the new-record button on every table screen was cut off the right edge, and a dead rule in the compiled stylesheet: React re-serialises inline styles with a space after the colon, so [style*="display:grid"] > * has never matched an element. Two gaps remain: below the 920px floor the main process enforces, the title bar's menu row can still overlap, and that overflow is computed in App.tsx rather than in CSS; and the per-screen narrow flag is still a per-control picker variant rather than part of the breakpoint system.

personal-vocabulary-upload.note: Corrected 2026-08-23, and the correction is the point: this row previously read "implemented -- fully wired into App.tsx", which was true of load, clear, status and storage and false of the one thing the feature exists to do. applyVocabularyText had no caller anywhere outside its own tests, so an uploaded file changed a validation status line and not one rendered word. Twelve assertions covered the function; none covered the wiring, which is why a green suite never noticed. It is now consumed through app/renderer/src/text-boundary.ts, which App.tsx hands the storage handle on mount, and tests/ui/text-boundary.test.tsx asserts a replacement actually reaches rendered text. Replacement runs after translation so a personal rename is the last word. app/renderer/src/personal-vocabulary.ts is imported and fully wired into App.tsx: file load (loadVocabularyFile), clear (clearVocabulary), status (vocabularyStatus) and storage. Corrected 2026-08-23: the durability gap noted then is fixed. The renderer no longer reaches window.localStorage (in-memory only for a file:// origin) for this cache; it now goes through app/renderer/src/durable-storage.ts, which write-through-caches against the main process's control-plane settings.snapshot/settings.write/settings.remove actions (control-plane/settings-store.ts), persisted atomically (control-plane/atomic-file.ts) to settings.json under app.getPath('userData') the way the server inventory already is. Proved by a real relaunch on a headless desktop: set a value, force-killed then gracefully closed the app, inspected settings.json on disk between runs, relaunched, and confirmed the restored value without any manual reload.

per-element-toy-locks.note: CORRECTED 2026-08-25: the previous note claimed two gaps that are now false. First, no OTP/TOTP option: the compiled lock wizard's lockMethods list genuinely offers three TOTP-including combinations -- 'PIN+TOTP', 'Password+TOTP', 'Password+PIN+TOTP' (generated/console.tsx near line 5690) -- and App.tsx's own lockNext/tryUnlock (overriding the generated design's PIN/password-only originals through the same App-extends-ConsoleShell mechanism used elsewhere) genuinely verify a real RFC 6238 code through totp.ts's verifyCode, refusing to finish a TOTP-including lock until pairAuth() has actually generated a secret (see built-in-authenticator.md for the pairing details). Second, no lock-creation wizard reachable from a documented context-menu command: 'Lock this element...' is a real, wired context-menu command with a shortcut hint (hint:'^L', generated/console.tsx line 5531) that opens the same lockOpen wizard, and it is documented below. The real gap this note should have named instead: the PIN, the password and the TOTP secret are all stored in plain React component state (state.locks, written and read directly in App.tsx's lockNext/tryUnlock), never in the OS credential vault -- confirmed by grepping the renderer for any vault/keytar/safeStorage reference near the lock mechanism and finding none. A toy lock is explicitly a for-fun speed bump rather than a security boundary, but the credential is still worth moving to the vault so a lock's PIN or password is not sitting in memory any more casually than it has to.

support-tickets.note: Implemented 2026-08-23 as app/renderer/src/support-tickets.ts with four controls in the design, filed through App.tsx. The joke desk is played straight -- category, severity nobody honours, a locally generated ticket number, a status that advances and stops at Resolved, a canned reply -- and the resolution opens the application-data folder so the person can delete it themselves. It never deletes anything: `action` is the literal "open-folder" rather than a boolean, because a field that could say delete-folder is one somebody eventually sets to it, and an in-app deletion would owe the two-key confirmation gate. One line is never styled by the funny level and states that nothing is sent anywhere, no data is collected and nobody is reading it, because a user waiting for a reply that was never coming is the only genuinely harmful outcome here. A scan refuses any copy naming a real desk or implying a response time. The consequence line restates that the reset clears every toy lock and that a toy lock was never security.

unlock-ladder.note: app/renderer/src/unlock-ladder.ts is now imported and wired into the real per-element unlock dialog (App.tsx authVals/tryUnlock/finishLadderGrade): after three consecutive wrong PIN/password/TOTP attempts on a lock, tryUnlock calls ladder.issue() and, for a real dish or sums challenge, reuses the dialog's existing numeric keypad/dots and its mono-font method line (no new markup added, since the compiled design has no bound slot for a dish grid or sums list) to collect and grade a real answer through ladder.grade(). Confirmed reachable in the built app: right-clicking a screen opens 'Lock this element...', which opens the real wizard. A cleared challenge only closes the ladder UI and says the wait is over -- it never touches state.locks or the unlock dialog's own PIN/password/TOTP buffers, so the real credential is still required afterward (rule 1). The module's own 3-per-hour skip budget, single-use graded nonces, and never-refunding-the-attempt-budget rules are enforced by the module itself, unmodified. Two real gaps remain, both because editing the compiled design/generated output was out of scope here: the 'moles' rung has no visual board to render in this build, so it is treated as unreachable and the ladder falls back to 'wait it out' rather than faking a graded round; and because this app's per-element lock has no server-enforced or time-based lockout of its own (unlike the PIN/password it sits beside), 'clearing the wait' here dismisses the ladder UI but does not bypass any actual timed lockout, since none exists to bypass.

built-in-authenticator.note: app/renderer/src/totp.ts is now imported and wired into the real per-element lock (App.tsx pairAuth/lockNext/tryUnlock/authVals). pairAuth generates a real random secret with the Web Crypto RNG, computes the real otpauth:// pairing URI (pairingUri), and reveals both as copyable text through the app's real info panel -- never a remote QR service, and never any network call. lockNext refuses to finish a TOTP-including lock until pairAuth has actually run, and stores the real secret (not a placeholder) in the lock record. tryUnlock verifies a real RFC 6238 code via verifyCode (one step of skew) using the app's own numeric keypad, reusing it for a second 'totp' entry phase after any PIN phase completes. Confirmed reachable in the built app via headless CDP: registered a real TOTP secret through the real UI, independently computed the current code from that exact captured secret with totp.ts's own generateCode, typed the six digits back into the running app's real unlock dialog, and the app's own verifyCode accepted it and cleared the lock -- an earlier, stale code was correctly rejected first. Two real gaps remain, both because editing the compiled design/generated output was out of scope here: the QR box next to 'Pair the built-in authenticator' is a static decorative gradient with no bound slot for pixel data (not S(v...) anywhere in it), so the secret is shown as copyable text instead of a scannable image; and there is no confirmation-code re-entry step before the secret is treated as paired, because the 'Password+TOTP' method's wizard panel has no digit-entry control of its own to collect one (the PIN keypad belongs to a different method combination and would corrupt the user's real PIN if reused for this). The secret itself is stored in the same non-durable, non-OS-credential-vault state.locks the PIN and password already were before this change -- a pre-existing gap, not a new one, and still recorded as such.

attention-modes.note: CORRECTED 2026-08-25: the previous note described the five toggles as though switching them on actually dimmed the interface, honoured motion preferences, or prompted about momentum -- none of that happens. What is real: five controls (att_focus, att_low, att_time, att_one, att_momentum) exist in the design, are off by default and independently toggleable, and App.tsx's setVal interception genuinely persists each one through isAttentionMode/setModeEnabled -- that half of the note was accurate. What is not real: attention-modes.ts also exports modeEnabled() (read a mode back), enabledModes(), presentationFor() (the function that would compute the actual dimming/low-stimulation/time-awareness presentation state), elapsedPhrase(), and momentumPrompt() (the function that would decide whether to show, and for how long to suppress, a momentum nudge). None of these five are imported by App.tsx, and a grep across the renderer finds no caller of any of them outside attention-modes.ts and its own test. So "Focus dims and never hides" and "Momentum respects a declined prompt for half an hour" describe code that exists and is tested, not behaviour a user can currently observe: flipping any of the five switches persists a boolean and changes nothing else in the running app. Nothing in the copy is medical, scored or judgemental, which the scan genuinely enforces -- that part of the claim stands.

browser-extension-download-surfaces.note: This is a desktop console for an Asterisk PBX; there is no browser extension in this repository and no Start-download/Downloading/complete dialog surfaces.

offline-documentation-browser.note: app/renderer/src/docs-browser.ts implements article lookup/search over the bundled docs, app/renderer/src/generated/docs-bundle.ts (83 articles) is real bundled content, and app/renderer/src/docs-markdown.ts parses each article's body into headings/paragraphs/code/list blocks with resolved inter-article links. The `docs` destination is now a real screen on the App rail (compiled from design/Asterisk Console M3.dc.html, kind:'docs') wired in App.tsx (docsVals) with a real search field, a regex-builder toggle and palette, an article list, a rendered body pane and in-app link navigation. Headlessly driven in the built app (Electron via CDP): the article list shows all 83 titles/excerpts, selecting an article renders its real headings/paragraphs (no raw '#'/'[]' Markdown syntax), an inline `[text](href)` link inside one article's body navigated to the linked article, and a query with no matches shows an honest '0 matches' state. Remaining gap: no promoted screenshot/interaction evidence has been filed under this project's design-parity capture pipeline, so this stays 'partial' rather than 'verified'.

app-display-name.note: CORRECTED 2026-08-25: the previous note claimed "a per-surface split so the chosen name reaches the title bar, About and notifications" -- that split (display-name.ts's exported nameFor(surface, storage), which is exactly the function that would decide per-surface which name to show) is never called anywhere. What is real: id_name and id_name_reset went into the design and came back through the compiler, App.tsx's setVal interception genuinely validates and persists a rename through setDisplayName/resetDisplayName, and the field is seeded from displayName(storage) on mount (restoreDisplayName, called once) -- the setting round-trips correctly. What is not real: the app/electron/main.ts BrowserWindow is created with a hard-coded `title: 'Ding PBX Console'` (line 163) that is never updated from the renderer's stored choice, there is no About screen or notification path that calls nameFor() or displayName() to render the chosen name, and displayName() itself is read back exactly once in the whole renderer -- to seed the settings field it came from. Renaming the console currently changes one settings field and nothing a user would see anywhere else; the title bar, About text and notifications all still say the shipped name. The safety property IS real and independently checked: IDENTITY is a frozen constant with no path from the display name, so a rename cannot orphan the application-data directory -- that half of the claim stands.

guided-forms.note: app/renderer/src/endpoint-create.ts (WIZARD_CONTROLS, buildEndpointDraft) is imported and wired into App.tsx (line 14, 482, 488) to drive the endpoint-creation wizard with real validated fields and a generated secret. This is a genuine guided form for one flow (new PJSIP endpoint), not a system-wide guided-forms contract.

bounded-overlays.note: Implemented 2026-08-24 as app/renderer/src/bounded-overlays.ts, consumed by App.tsx as of 2026-08-25: a pure placement calculator returning position, constrained size, whether the overlay scrolls internally, and which side of the anchor it landed on, plus a surface check that refuses an overlay declaring no background, border, elevation or shape. Reached without hand-editing the compiled design by overriding App's own setState (boundedOverlaySetState) and showInfo (styledShowInfo) rather than editing console.tsx: every click handler in the compiled design that opens the context menu sets ctxX/ctxY together, in one plain object, as raw `${e.clientX}px`/`${e.clientY}px` with no bound against the window anywhere (`position:absolute; left:${ctxX}; top:${ctxY}` in console.tsx) -- computeOverlayPlacement now clamps that pair into the real window viewport before the compiled shell's real setState ever sees it, treating the click point as a zero-size anchor and the menu's own fixed width plus a generous height estimate as the desired size. lockX/lockY and regexX/regexY copy ctxX/ctxY the moment they open (`lockX:s.ctxX, lockY:s.ctxY`), so they inherit the clamp for free. showInfo's own click-anchored call site (the ctx menu's "Explain this..." item) is clamped the same way at the wrapper that already exists to style its copy. 18 tests plus this consumption.

context-menu-shortcuts.note: Implemented 2026-08-24 as app/renderer/src/menu-shortcuts.ts: a registry that resolves the binding which actually fires a command IN THAT CONTEXT, so a shortcut from another surface is never displayed and one is never inferred from a similarly named command. An item with no binding shows nothing rather than a placeholder, the chord is exposed as a shortcut rather than glued into the label, and two commands sharing a chord in one context is reported as a conflict rather than silently resolved. 17 tests. Its conflict grouping compares context and chord directly rather than joining them into a string key: the first version used a separator that reached the file as a literal NUL. The module is complete and its guards are proven, but NOTHING IMPORTS IT YET -- no surface in the renderer calls it, so today it constrains nothing that ships. Recorded as partial rather than implemented for exactly that reason: a module wired at one end and consumed at neither is the defect this project has shipped a dozen times, and marking it done would be that same claim.
context-menu-shortcuts.blockedBy: BLOCKED ON THE COMPILED MENUS. The context menus are rendered by the compiled design, which cannot be hand-edited, so displaying a resolved chord on a menu item means the design emitting a shortcut slot the registry can fill. That is a compiler change rather than a wiring change.

long-operation-progress.note: Implemented 2026-08-24 as app/renderer/src/long-operation-progress.ts, consumed by App.tsx as of 2026-08-25: weighted phases producing real fractional progress, a re-entry guard that refuses a second start and says it refused, determinate versus indeterminate state distinguishable from stalled, a stall detector, and cancellation reporting partial completion honestly. The earlier blocker was that provisioning is really TWO fixed step sequences (dispatch.ts picks provisioning.provision(true) or provisioning.provisionFromBaseImage() up front, depending on whether this build carries the packaged payload) and one plan cannot describe both without reportProgress throwing on an unrecognised or out-of-order phase. Resolved with two separate phase lists (DEPLOY_PHASES, DEPLOY_PHASES_FROM_BASE_IMAGE) plus firstStepPlan, which reads the very first onProvisionStep call to pick the one the run actually opened -- resetDeployProgress starts against the packaged-payload plan as a placeholder, since which sequence will run is not known before the request, and onProvisionStep swaps in the correct plan on the first step if that guess was wrong, before anything has been banked. A 2-second ticker (deployTicker) recomputes the percentage and stall message while running, since `wsl --import`/the base-image download can run silent for minutes between steps -- a step-boundary-only refresh would never show a stall during the one phase it matters most for. A step name neither plan recognises degrades to plain step text with no percentage rather than throwing at the user. 38 tests plus this consumption.

in-context-recovery.note: Implemented 2026-08-24 as app/renderer/src/in-context-recovery.ts, consumed by App on the deploy-failure path -- a failing provisioning step now offers a route out rather than leaving somebody holding an error string. The property that matters is what it refuses: a rejected push has remedies that look fast and destroy commits (force-push, reset, dropping the branch, switching mid-conflict), and those are named as forbidden rather than merely left out, so a caller handing the situation to a coding agent passes the prohibition on rather than only the goal. A refused permission offers no retry, because repeating a refused action changes nothing and reads as the console not having understood the answer. An unrecognised failure says so and shows the full error instead of a cheerful "Try again" that fails the same way. The real error is carried through every branch rather than replaced by the summary, since a summary that swallowed it leaves somebody unable to search for what happened. Failures are classified on the reported detail rather than the step name, because the name says what was attempted and the detail says why it did not work.

provider-markup-rendering.note: app/renderer/src/docs-markdown.ts parses bundled documentation body text (headings, paragraphs, fenced code, bullet list items, inline `[text](href)` links) into render-ready blocks, and the `docs` screen (App.tsx docsVals + the compiled `isDocs` template block) renders those blocks as real UI rather than printing raw Markdown source — confirmed by headless capture of the running app. This covers the bundled offline docs only; there is still no renderer for remote-authored text such as release notes or issue bodies.

forge-publishing.note: Implemented 2026-08-24 as app/renderer/src/forge-publishing.ts: multi-account sign-in with an active account that keeps single-account callers working, owner selection across a user’s own namespace and the organizations they can create in, route selection between forking and copy-and-push, and a plan that reports every problem at once. No token passes through the module: an account carries only the vault key naming where its token lives, asserted both against the object and against the type declaration -- the object-level check alone missed an optional field added to the interface, which is how that gap was found. With several accounts signed in and none chosen, nothing is active rather than the first being guessed, because guessing is how work lands in somebody else’s namespace and is discovered by a colleague not finding it. A fork preference on a forge that cannot fork becomes a copy and SAYS SO, since a fork has an upstream link and a copy does not.
forge-publishing.blockedBy: BLOCKED ON THE FORGE TRANSPORT. The module decides what should happen and nothing performs it: there is no code that calls a forge API to create a repository, fork one, or push to a new remote, and no account list for it to read. Real consumption needs the privileged process to own those calls -- the renderer must not hold a token -- exposed the way the provisioning steps now are, plus an account store keyed to the OS credential vault. Until then this is a correct decision it has no way to carry out, and wiring a control to it would produce a publish button that plans and never publishes.

collapsible-filters.note: Implemented 2026-08-24 as app/renderer/src/collapsible-filters.ts: panel kinds with their default collapsed state (statistics start collapsed, since a view whose controls occupy more space than its content has buried the content), persistence, and the rule that matters most -- a collapsed panel currently EXCLUDING results must say so, because a quietly filtering collapsed row is how somebody comes to believe their data is missing. 30 tests. The module is complete and its guards are proven, but NOTHING IMPORTS IT YET -- no surface in the renderer calls it, so today it constrains nothing that ships. Recorded as partial rather than implemented for exactly that reason: a module wired at one end and consumed at neither is the defect this project has shipped a dozen times, and marking it done would be that same claim.
collapsible-filters.blockedBy: BLOCKED ON A CONSUMER. No surface in the console renders a collapsible panel, so the drafted controls would write real storage keys that nothing reads. Real consumption means a screen with a filter row or a statistics panel calling isCollapsed and setCollapsed with its own surface id, and rendering the active-filter summary when a filtering panel is collapsed. The module also needs to export its per-surface storage-key helper, or an enumeration, before any status readback is possible -- today only the prefix is exported, so a caller cannot reconstruct which panels exist.

automatic-updates.note: app/renderer/src/UpdateBanner.tsx (64 lines) is mounted as its own root in main.tsx (lines 39-41) and control-plane/updater.ts implements the update-check/download/ready-to-restart backend. Genuinely wired: the banner is created and rendered on every boot alongside the main app.
